meta.title: Who really said "We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Vonnegut — but not from the novel’s story. He wrote it in the introduction he added to Mother Night in 1966, four years after publication.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be'?
meta.ogDescription: Vonnegut really wrote it — in the 1966 introduction to Mother Night, not in the novel itself. Often misquoted with the clauses reversed.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Vonnegut wrote this one himself — but not in the story. It appears in the introduction he added to Mother Night in 1966, four years after the novel first appeared in February 1962. Wikiquote ↗ files the line under the novel and marks it “Introduction (1966)”, and Wikipedia’s article on Vonnegut ↗ independently reports that he “wrote in a foreword to a later edition” the same sentence.

source.excerpt: We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced listing for Vonnegut ↗ places the exact wording under Mother Night and pins it specifically to the “Introduction (1966)” — not to the novel’s narrative.
Wikipedia’s Vonnegut article ↗ independently reports that he “wrote in a foreword to a later edition” the identical sentence, citing Charles J. Shields’s biography And So It Goes (2011), pp. 171–173.

Wikipedia’s article on Mother Night ↗ dates the novel’s first publication to February 1962, from Fawcett Publications / Gold Medal Books — so the line people quote as the book’s moral was written four years after the book.
The same Wikiquote entry ↗ also records the line’s common corruption, “Be careful what you pretend to be because you are what you pretend to be”, which reverses Vonnegut’s clause order.
source.excerptNote: The sentence as Wikiquote records it from the 1966 introduction. We have not reproduced the surrounding paragraph: the introduction is still in copyright and no copy we could open was available to transcribe its context, so nothing beyond the sentence itself is quoted here.
source.rightsNote: Mother Night was first published in 1962 and the introduction carrying this line was added in 1966. Both are far too recent for the United States public domain, which currently reaches works published through 1930, so the text remains under copyright.

author.name: Kurt Vonnegut
author.heading: About Kurt Vonnegut
author.bio: Kurt Vonnegut survived the firebombing of Dresden as a prisoner of war and spent the next fifty years writing about it, most directly in Slaughterhouse-Five. Mother Night (1962) is his bleakest joke: a novel about a spy so good at pretending to be a Nazi that the distinction stops meaning anything. He is one of the most quotable American novelists of the century, which also makes him one of the most frequently misquoted.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this is Vonnegut. What goes wrong is the wording, and where in the book people think it comes from.

items.who: “Be careful what you pretend to be because you are what you pretend to be”
items.why: A widely circulated rewrite that flips Vonnegut’s clause order and drops his “so we must”. Wikiquote ↗ lists it explicitly as a misquotation of the line.

The sentence is not spoken by Howard W. Campbell Jr. or by any character: Wikiquote ↗ places it in the author’s own introduction, which Wikipedia ↗ describes as a foreword written for a later edition — dated 1966 by Wikiquote, four years after the 1962 first publication ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The safe way to quote it: Kurt Vonnegut, introduction to Mother Night (1966) — not the 1962 novel proper. See Wikiquote’s entry ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Mother Night is the story of Howard W. Campbell Jr., an American playwright who stays on in Germany and becomes the radio voice of Nazi propaganda aimed at Americans — while passing coded messages to American intelligence in the deliberate pauses and coughs of his own broadcasts. He turns out to have been a very effective propagandist either way. The moral lands hard because the book refuses to let him off on the grounds that he did not mean it.

That is also why the sentence travels so well without the novel attached. Stripped of Campbell, it reads as ordinary advice about habits and self-image; in context it is a much colder claim — that the performance is the person, and sincerity buys you nothing.
detailsBody: Vonnegut added the introduction to a later edition, four years after the novel first appeared, and used it to state a moral outright. Campbell tells his own story from a cell in an Israeli prison while he waits for a war-crimes trial — so the sentence readers take as the book’s lesson reaches them from outside that story, in Vonnegut’s own voice rather than his narrator’s.
context.pull: The performance is the person — sincerity buys you nothing.
